title: A Autopsy for the Witness
premise: Yara Vane, the coroner of rain-soaked Hollowmere, is called to examine a body pulled from the reservoir and recognizes it as Marisol Quade, a woman who vanished three years ago. The twist: Marisol's recovered diary contains entries written after her disappearance, in her handwriting, describing Yara's own investigation in real time. As Yara follows the diary's trail, they discover Marisol faked her death to escape the town's founding family, who have been quietly inheriting land through staged deaths for generations — and that the diary's final blank pages are an invitation. To close the case, Yara must let the killer believe they've won, staging their own autopsy while the true heir's confession is recorded beneath the mortuary floor.
about_author: Xanthe Thackeray spent a decade transcribing inquest records in coastal England before turning to fiction, a job that taught her how often the dead outtalk the living. She writes mysteries about small towns where everyone remembers everything except what matters.

chapters.title: The Reservoir Gives Up Its Dead
chapters.summary: Yara Vane performs an autopsy on a body dredged from Hollowmere reservoir and identifies it as Marisol Quade, missing three years — yet the decomposition timeline doesn't match. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: professional confidence beginning to crack; the first wrong note in a file Yara prides themselves on knowing completely.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Searching Marisol's sealed effects, Yara finds her diary — with entries dated months after her disappearance, describing the reservoir recovery before it happened. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: vertigo and denial; the investigator realizes they are being read even as they read.

chapters.title: A Town That Remembers Wrong
chapters.summary: Yara canvasses old neighbors and finds the town's memory of Marisol suspiciously uniform, as if rehearsed. Deputy Ilsa Brand warns them off gently. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: loneliness sharpening into resolve; belonging in Hollowmere suddenly feels like a debt.

chapters.title: The Quade Inheritance
chapters.summary: Land records reveal three Quade-family deaths across a century, each followed by the Ashcombe founders acquiring the property cheaply. POV: alternating Yara and archival documents. Emotional beat: cold wonder — the pattern is generational, patient, and still operating.

chapters.title: What the Diary Predicts
chapters.summary: The diary describes Yara's visit to the boathouse hours before it occurs. Yara goes anyway and finds a fresh footprint matching their own boot size. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: fear curdling into defiance; someone wants Yara to feel hunted.

chapters.title: The Founder's Grandson
chapters.summary: Yara interviews Edmund Ashcombe, charming heir to the estate, who quotes details of the autopsy never made public. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: the mask slips just enough; power here wears good tailoring and knows your name.

chapters.title: Ilsa's Quiet File
chapters.summary: Yara discovers Deputy Brand has kept an unofficial folder on the Ashcombes for years — including a photo of Marisol alive, eight months ago, at a bus depot two counties away. POV: Ilsa, then Yara. Emotional beat: reluctant alliance; trust extended cautiously between two people trained to suspect.

chapters.title: Alive, Then
chapters.summary: Following the depot lead, Yara learns Marisol was hiding from her own family, who sold her inheritance rights to the Ashcombes after her 'death.' POV: Yara. Emotional beat: grief inverted — the dead woman is alive, which makes the reservoir body someone else's tragedy.

chapters.title: The Second Body
chapters.summary: A drifter is found dead with Marisol's ID; dental records confirm the reservoir victim was never Marisol at all. Someone supplied a substitute corpse. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: horror deepening — the killer can manufacture death itself, and chose to.

chapters.title: Who Signs a Death Certificate
chapters.summary: Yara traces the paperwork: the fake identity was certified by Yara's own predecessor, now retired and terrified, who confesses to one falsified document under pressure from the estate. POV: Yara and the predecessor. Emotional beat: complicity everywhere; corruption as inheritance, passed down like silverware.

chapters.title: The Diary Changes Hands
chapters.summary: The diary vanishes from Yara's locked office and reappears on their porch, now containing a new entry: an address, a time, and the words 'come alone or she finishes what you started.' POV: Yara. Emotional beat: the trap closes; the reader has become the read.

chapters.title: Ashcombe House at Night
chapters.summary: Yara breaks into the estate and finds a room of files documenting every staged death since 1890 — and a recent photograph of Marisol, alive, held somewhere on the grounds. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: awe and dread; the house is an archive of perfected murder.

chapters.title: Caught in the Family Way
chapters.summary: Edmund catches Yara but lets them go, delivering a velvet threat about Yara's own precarious position in a town that employs them at the council's pleasure. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: humiliation and clarity; power corrupts most efficiently through permission.

chapters.title: Marisol Speaks
chapters.summary: Using Ilsa's contacts, Yara reaches Marisol, who reveals she wrote the post-disappearance entries herself — coached by someone inside the Ashcombe house who wanted the pattern exposed. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: hope with a hairline fracture; every ally might be bait.

chapters.title: The Inside Hand
chapters.summary: Yara deduces the inside informant is the estate's archivist, Ruth Ashcombe-Byrne, Edmund's aunt — who has been feeding evidence to Marisol while playing loyal. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: the board revealed; three players, each convinced they're setting the trap.

chapters.title: Deadline in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Ruth contacts Yara: the next staged death is scheduled within days — hers — unless the pattern is exposed publicly first. She hands over the master ledger. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: desperation of the complicit trying to buy redemption with stolen paper.

chapters.title: The Trap Reversed
chapters.summary: Edmund discovers the theft, takes Marisol hostage, and summons Yara with a message written in the diary's style: he has always been the author. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: rage and terror fused; the killer knew the file because he wrote it, generation after generation.

chapters.title: An Autopsy for the Witness
chapters.summary: Yara proposes the unthinkable: stage their own death certificate, letting Edmund believe his machine has claimed its latest victim, drawing him to the mortuary to destroy the evidence personally. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: cold courage; the coroner will lie among the dead to catch the living.

chapters.title: The Long Table
chapters.summary: In the mortuary, Yara lies under a sheet while Edmund arrives to burn the ledger; hidden recorders capture his full confession as he gloats over the 'body.' He pulls back the sheet. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: the held breath of the climax; eye contact with a murderer who thinks he owns death.

chapters.title: What the Dead Heard
chapters.summary: Ilsa and state police move in; Edmund, exposed, tries to burn the archive and is arrested amid the smoke of his family's century of paper. Marisol is freed. POV: Ilsa. Emotional beat: catharsis; the machinery of inherited power jammed by its own arrogance.

chapters.title: Closing the File
chapters.summary: Yara signs corrected certificates for every staged death, giving the long-dead their true names back, and testifies as the ledger becomes public record. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: restitution; belonging earned not by silence but by truth-telling.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Yara walks the cemetery at dusk, renaming headstones aloud, and finds a new diary on their doorstep — blank, with a note: 'In case you ever need a witness.' POV: Yara. Emotional beat: quiet, wary peace; the case closed, the habit of watching forever changed.
